1	# Invention disclosure (the inventor's own words)
2	
3	This is the ONLY authority for what the invention includes. Everything you claim must be supported here or in later messages from the user.
4	
5	A reusable inline liquid metering valve delivers a repeatable dose of concentrate into a flowing carrier liquid and automatically rinses the surfaces that contacted the concentrate after each dose. The valve has a cylindrical housing with an inlet at one axial end and an outlet at the opposite axial end. A metering sleeve is fixed inside the housing. The sleeve defines a cylindrical dose chamber, a radial concentrate port, a carrier-liquid admission port, and a flush bypass that opens downstream of the dose chamber.
6	
7	A piston slides axially in the dose chamber between a fill position and a discharge position. The piston has two axially spaced sealing lands joined by a reduced-diameter waist. In the fill position, the waist connects the concentrate port to the dose chamber while both lands isolate the carrier-liquid path. Movement to the discharge position closes the concentrate port before the downstream land uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port. Carrier liquid then enters behind the measured volume and expels that volume through a one-way outlet valve into the main flow. The ordering of the port edges and lands prevents the concentrate source from communicating directly with the carrier-liquid inlet.
8	
9	An index collar surrounds the metering sleeve and has a helical cam groove engaged by a follower pin carried by the piston rod. Each full piston stroke turns the index collar by one increment. Three selectable axial stop faces on the collar set three dose volumes by limiting piston travel. A spring-biased detent engages one of three recesses to retain the selected setting. A transparent window in the housing shows one of three reference numerals carried on the collar, so the dose setting is mechanically visible without electronics.
10	
11	When the piston returns toward the fill position, a flexible lip on the upstream sealing land first wipes the dose-chamber wall. Near the end of the return stroke, the follower pin opens a normally closed flush poppet connected to the flush bypass. Carrier liquid flows through an annular rinse channel between the sleeve and housing, through two radial rinse openings directed across the concentrate port and the one-way outlet valve, and then through the flush bypass to the outlet. The flush poppet closes before the waist reconnects the concentrate port. A replaceable cartridge contains the piston, metering sleeve, one-way outlet valve, and flush poppet and is retained by a threaded end cap. Removing the end cap withdraws the cartridge without disturbing the housing connections. An apparatus claim and a method claim should cover the ordered isolation, metering, discharge, and automatic rinse sequence.

Many liquid handling installations add a small, accurately measured quantity of a concentrate to a much larger stream of a carrier liquid that is already flowing in a pipe. The concentrate may be aggressive, staining, strongly coloured, biologically active, or simply expensive, and the quantity that must be added is small in comparison with the carrier flow. The addition therefore has to be made repeatably, without measuring the concentrate by eye, and without allowing the concentrate to reach any part of the installation other than the carrier stream itself.

Two practical difficulties dominate this kind of dosing. The first is separation of the two liquids upstream of the point of addition. A dosing device sits between a concentrate source and a pressurised carrier line, and any path that momentarily connects the two allows carrier liquid to be forced back into the concentrate source or allows concentrate to migrate into the carrier line at a time when no dose is called for. Devices that rely on separately actuated shut-off elements to keep the two sides apart depend on those elements being commanded in the correct order, so a control fault, a lost signal, or a slow-acting element can open both sides at once.

The second difficulty is residue. The surfaces that the concentrate touches, in particular the port through which it enters the metering volume and the seat of the check element through which the dose leaves, retain a film of concentrate after the dose has been delivered. That film drips into the carrier stream between doses, so the quantity actually added is not the quantity that was measured. It also dries, crystallises, or reacts on the wetted surfaces, so that a valve which was accurate when new drifts, sticks, or seizes in service. The usual remedy is to break the valve out of the line and clean it by hand, which takes the installation out of service and exposes the person doing the work to the concentrate. Where a rinse is provided at all, it is commonly a separate operation that has to be commanded after the dose, and it therefore depends on an operator or a controller performing an extra step at the right moment.

Dose selection presents a further difficulty. Adjustable dosing devices are often set by a screw or by an electronically stored value. A screw setting can be lost during cleaning and gives no indication of what was set. An electronic setting requires power, a sensor and a display at the valve, which is unwelcome in wet, washdown or hazardous locations, and it tells the operator only what the controller believes rather than what the mechanism will actually deliver.

There remains a need for an inline metering valve in which the separation of the concentrate from the carrier liquid is enforced by the geometry of the moving parts rather than by the order in which external commands arrive, in which the surfaces wetted by the concentrate are rinsed by the carrier liquid as an unavoidable part of the return of the metering element, and in which the selected dose is both retained and displayed mechanically.

An inline liquid metering valve delivers a repeatable measured volume of concentrate into a flowing carrier liquid and rinses the surfaces that contacted the concentrate after each dose, without electrical power and without any command additional to the stroke that delivers the dose.

The valve has a housing with an inlet and an outlet and a metering sleeve fixed within the housing. The metering sleeve defines a dose chamber, a concentrate port opening into the dose chamber, a carrier-liquid admission port opening into the dose chamber, and a flush bypass that opens downstream of the dose chamber. A piston slides axially in the dose chamber between a fill position and a discharge position. The piston has an upstream sealing land and a downstream sealing land axially spaced from one another and joined by a reduced-diameter waist.

Separation of the two liquids is enforced by the axial order of the land faces and the port edges rather than by the sequence in which any external command arrives. In the fill position, the waist connects the concentrate port to the dose chamber while the upstream and downstream sealing lands isolate the carrier-liquid admission port from the concentrate port. Movement of the piston toward the discharge position closes the concentrate port before the downstream sealing land uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port. Carrier liquid then enters behind the measured volume of concentrate and expels that volume through a one-way outlet valve toward the outlet. Because one land face has passed the concentrate port before the other land face releases the carrier-liquid admission port, no position of the piston places the concentrate source in communication with the carrier-liquid path.

The rinse is carried out by the return of the same piston. An annular rinse channel lies between an outer surface of the metering sleeve and an inner surface of the housing, and at least one rinse opening leads from that channel through the metering sleeve into the dose chamber. A follower pin carried by the piston rod opens a normally closed flush poppet connected to the flush bypass during the return stroke, so that carrier liquid sweeps the annular rinse channel, issues from the rinse opening across the surfaces wetted by the concentrate, and leaves through the flush bypass to the outlet. The flush poppet closes before the waist reconnects the concentrate port to the dose chamber, so the rinse is complete, and the rinse liquid is on its way to the outlet, before any further concentrate can enter. The rinse cannot be omitted, mistimed or deferred, because the element that opens it is the element that carries the piston.

In described embodiments, a flexible lip on the upstream sealing land wipes the wall of the dose chamber before the flush poppet opens, so that the flushing stream is presented with a film rather than with standing liquid. Two radial rinse openings are directed across the concentrate port and across the one-way outlet valve, which are the two surfaces on which residue is otherwise retained.

Dose selection is mechanical and self-indexing. An index collar surrounds the metering sleeve and has a helical cam groove engaged by the follower pin, so that each full stroke of the piston turns the index collar by one increment. Three selectable axial stop faces on the index collar limit the travel of the piston and thereby set three dose volumes, a spring-biased detent engaging one of three recesses retains the selected setting, and a transparent window in the housing shows one of three dose setting indicia carried by the index collar, so that the setting is visible without electronics.

A replaceable cartridge contains the piston, the metering sleeve, the one-way outlet valve and the flush poppet, and is retained by a threaded end cap. Removing the threaded end cap withdraws the cartridge without disturbing the connections at the inlet and the outlet.

A corresponding method admits concentrate to the dose chamber, closes the concentrate port before uncovering the carrier-liquid admission port, expels the measured volume through the one-way outlet valve, and then opens the flush poppet with the follower pin during the return of the piston and closes it again before the concentrate port is reconnected.

In the following description, the terms upstream and downstream refer to the direction of travel of the carrier liquid from the inlet toward the outlet, and the terms axial and radial refer to the axis along which the piston slides.

Overall arrangement

FIG. 1 shows an inline liquid metering valve 10. The inline liquid metering valve 10 has a cylindrical housing 12 with an inlet 14 at one axial end and an outlet 16 at the opposite axial end, so that the inline liquid metering valve 10 can be connected in a line that already carries a flowing carrier liquid. The carrier liquid enters at the inlet 14, passes along the housing 12, and leaves at the outlet 16. This flow of carrier liquid past the metering parts is the main flow into which each dose of concentrate is delivered, and it is also the only liquid used to rinse the valve.

A metering sleeve 18 is fixed within the housing 12 and is spaced radially inward from the inner surface of the housing 12 over part of its length. A piston 28 is carried within the metering sleeve 18. The metering sleeve 18, the piston 28 and the valve elements described below are assembled together as a cartridge 64, which is retained in the housing 12 by a threaded end cap 66. The cartridge 64 is described further below.

Metering sleeve, ports and piston

Referring to FIG. 2, the metering sleeve 18 defines a dose chamber 20, a concentrate port 22 opening into the dose chamber 20, a carrier-liquid admission port 24 opening into the dose chamber 20, and a flush bypass 26 that opens downstream of the dose chamber 20. The dose chamber 20 is cylindrical. The concentrate port 22 is a radial port through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 and is connected in use to a concentrate source. The carrier-liquid admission port 24 is a radial port through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 at an axial position downstream of the concentrate port 22 and admits carrier liquid to the dose chamber 20.

The piston 28 is axially slidable in the dose chamber 20 between a fill position and a discharge position. The piston 28 has an upstream sealing land 30 and a downstream sealing land 32 axially spaced from one another and joined by a reduced-diameter waist 34. Each sealing land bears on the wall of the dose chamber 20, while the waist 34 stands clear of that wall and so forms an annular space that travels with the piston 28. A piston rod 36 extends from the piston 28 along the axis of the dose chamber 20 and is arranged to be driven through a stroke and a return stroke by an external actuating member, whether a hand lever, a pneumatic or hydraulic actuator, or any other source of reciprocating motion. A one-way outlet valve 38 is arranged to pass liquid from the dose chamber 20 toward the outlet 16 and to prevent flow in the opposite direction. The one-way outlet valve 38 may take any form that passes liquid in one direction only, such as a ball or disc urged onto a seat or a resiliently biased closure element.

Ordered isolation and metering

FIG. 2 shows the piston 28 in the fill position. In the fill position the waist 34 connects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20, and the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 isolate the carrier-liquid admission port 24 from the concentrate port 22. Concentrate accordingly passes from the concentrate source through the concentrate port 22 and into the dose chamber 20, where it occupies the annular space at the waist 34 and forms a measured volume of concentrate. Throughout the fill position the carrier-liquid path is closed to the concentrate, because the downstream sealing land 32 overlies the carrier-liquid admission port 24 and the upstream sealing land 30 closes the dose chamber 20 on the other side of the waist 34.

Movement of the piston 28 toward the discharge position closes the concentrate port 22 before the downstream sealing land 32 uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port 24. The upstream sealing land 30 arrives at the concentrate port 22 and shuts it while the downstream sealing land 32 is still overlying the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Only after that has happened does continued travel of the piston 28 carry the downstream sealing land 32 clear of the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Carrier liquid then enters through the carrier-liquid admission port 24 behind the measured volume of concentrate in the dose chamber 20 and expels the measured volume through the one-way outlet valve 38 toward the outlet 16, where it joins the main flow.

The axial ordering of the faces of the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 relative to the edges of the concentrate port 22 and the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is chosen so that the concentrate port 22 is closed at every piston position at which the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is open. There is accordingly no position of the piston 28 at which the concentrate source communicates directly with the carrier-liquid path. The separation of the two liquids is a property of the geometry of the piston 28 and the metering sleeve 18 and does not depend on the order in which any external command is given, on any control signal, or on the correct operation of any separately actuated shut-off element. A slow stroke, an interrupted stroke or a stroke reversed part way through cannot open both ports at once, because the port that must close does so at an earlier point on the same continuous path of travel than the port that then opens.

Dose selection by the index collar

Referring to FIG. 4, an index collar 40 surrounds the metering sleeve 18 and has a helical cam groove 42 engaged by a follower pin 44 carried by the piston rod 36. Each full stroke of the piston 28 draws the follower pin 44 along the helical cam groove 42 and turns the index collar 40 by one increment, so that the index collar 40 advances by itself as the valve is used and needs no separate indexing drive.

Three selectable axial stop faces 46 are carried by the index collar 40 at different axial positions. The stop face presented by the current increment of rotation limits the travel of the piston 28 and thereby sets the dose volume, so that the three axial stop faces 46 correspond to three dose volumes. A spring-biased detent 48 engages one of three detent recesses 50 to retain the selected setting, so that the index collar 40 is held against vibration and against the forces transmitted through the follower pin 44 until it is next indexed.

A transparent window 52 in the housing 12 shows one of three dose setting indicia 54 carried by the index collar 40. The dose setting indicium presented at the transparent window 52 is the one associated with the axial stop face currently limiting the travel of the piston 28, so the dose setting is mechanically visible without electronics, without power at the valve and without a controller. What the window shows is the position of the mechanism itself rather than a stored value, so the displayed setting cannot disagree with the volume the valve will deliver.

Wiping and automatic rinse

FIG. 3 shows the metering portion during the return stroke of the piston 28 toward the fill position. A flexible lip 56 is carried on the upstream sealing land 30 and bears on the wall of the dose chamber 20. As the return stroke begins, the flexible lip 56 wipes the wall of the dose chamber 20 and carries the film of concentrate remaining on that wall ahead of it, so that the rinse that follows is presented with a wetted surface rather than with standing liquid.

An annular rinse channel 60 lies between an outer surface of the metering sleeve 18 and an inner surface of the housing 12 and is supplied with carrier liquid from the inlet 14. Two radial rinse openings 62 pass through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 and connect the annular rinse channel 60 to the dose chamber 20. One of the two radial rinse openings 62 is directed across the concentrate port 22 and the other is directed across the one-way outlet valve 38. These are the two surfaces on which concentrate is otherwise retained after a dose, the first because concentrate stands in the mouth of the port and the second because concentrate is the last liquid to pass the seat.

A normally closed flush poppet 58 is connected to the flush bypass 26. Near the end of the return stroke, the follower pin 44 reaches the flush poppet 58 and opens it. Carrier liquid then flows from the inlet 14 through the annular rinse channel 60, through the two radial rinse openings 62 across the concentrate port 22 and the one-way outlet valve 38, and through the flush bypass 26 to the outlet 16. The rinse liquid therefore leaves by the same route as the dose and is carried away in the main flow.

The flush poppet 58 closes before the waist 34 reconnects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20. The concentrate port 22 is closed throughout the interval in which the annular rinse channel 60 communicates with the flush bypass 26, so that carrier liquid under the pressure of the main line is never presented to an open concentrate port and cannot be driven back toward the concentrate source. Only when the flush poppet 58 has closed does the continuing return of the piston 28 bring the waist 34 back into register with the concentrate port 22, at which point the dose chamber 20 is charged again for the next dose.

Because the follower pin 44 that opens the flush poppet 58 is carried by the piston rod 36, the rinse happens once for every dose and at the same point in every cycle. It is not a separate operation, it needs no command, and it cannot be omitted while the valve continues to be used. The rinse also occurs while the concentrate port 22 is shut and after the wall of the dose chamber 20 has been wiped, so it removes a film with clean carrier liquid rather than diluting a standing charge of concentrate.

Cartridge and service

Referring again to FIG. 1, the cartridge 64 contains the piston 28, the metering sleeve 18, the one-way outlet valve 38 and the flush poppet 58, and is retained in the housing 12 by the threaded end cap 66. Removing the threaded end cap 66 withdraws the cartridge 64 from the housing 12 along the axis of the dose chamber 20 without disturbing the connections at the inlet 14 and the outlet 16, so that the wearing and sealing parts can be replaced as a unit while the housing 12 remains in the line. The parts of the cartridge 64 that contact the concentrate are the parts that are exchanged, so a change of concentrate or a worn sealing land is dealt with by fitting a further cartridge rather than by dismantling the installation.

The materials of the metering sleeve 18, the piston 28, the flexible lip 56 and the sealing elements are selected for compatibility with the carrier liquid and with the concentrate to be dosed. The spring-biased detent 48 may be a spring-loaded ball or a spring-loaded plunger, and the flexible lip 56 may be formed integrally with the upstream sealing land 30 or as a separate resilient element retained on it.

Operation

In use, carrier liquid flows through the housing 12 from the inlet 14 to the outlet 16. With the piston 28 in the fill position, concentrate is admitted through the concentrate port 22 and past the waist 34 into the dose chamber 20 to form a measured volume, the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 isolating the carrier-liquid admission port 24 from the concentrate port 22. The piston 28 is then advanced toward the discharge position so as to close the concentrate port 22 and thereafter to uncover the carrier-liquid admission port 24 with the downstream sealing land 32. Carrier liquid is admitted through the carrier-liquid admission port 24 behind the measured volume and expels the measured volume through the one-way outlet valve 38 toward the outlet 16. The travel of the piston 28 on this stroke is limited by the selected one of the three axial stop faces 46, which sets the measured volume.

The piston 28 is then returned toward the fill position. During the return, the flexible lip 56 on the upstream sealing land 30 wipes the wall of the dose chamber 20, and the follower pin 44 carried by the piston rod 36 opens the normally closed flush poppet 58. Carrier liquid flows through the annular rinse channel 60 between the metering sleeve 18 and the housing 12, through the two radial rinse openings 62 in the metering sleeve 18 across the concentrate port 22 and the one-way outlet valve 38, and through the flush bypass 26 that opens downstream of the dose chamber 20 to the outlet 16. The flush poppet 58 is closed before the waist 34 reconnects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20. Over the same full stroke, the follower pin 44 travelling in the helical cam groove 42 turns the index collar 40 by one increment, the spring-biased detent 48 enters the next of the three detent recesses 50, and the dose setting indicium then presented at the transparent window 52 shows the setting that will govern the next dose. The valve is thereby left charged, rinsed and set, ready for the following cycle.

In the following description, the terms upstream and downstream refer to the direction of travel of the carrier liquid from the inlet toward the outlet, and the terms axial and radial refer to the axis along which the piston slides.

Overall arrangement

FIG. 1 shows an inline liquid metering valve 10. The inline liquid metering valve 10 has a cylindrical housing 12 with an inlet 14 at one axial end and an outlet 16 at the opposite axial end, so that the inline liquid metering valve 10 can be connected in a line that already carries a flowing carrier liquid. The carrier liquid enters at the inlet 14, passes along the housing 12, and leaves at the outlet 16. This flow of carrier liquid past the metering parts is the main flow into which each dose of concentrate is delivered, and it is also the only liquid used to rinse the valve.

A metering sleeve 18 is fixed within the housing 12 and is spaced radially inward from the inner surface of the housing 12 over part of its length. A piston 28 is carried within the metering sleeve 18. The metering sleeve 18, the piston 28 and the valve elements described below are assembled together as a cartridge 64, which is retained in the housing 12 by a threaded end cap 66. The cartridge 64 is described further below.

Metering sleeve, ports and piston

Referring to FIG. 2, the metering sleeve 18 defines a dose chamber 20, a concentrate port 22 opening into the dose chamber 20, a carrier-liquid admission port 24 opening into the dose chamber 20, and a flush bypass 26 that opens downstream of the dose chamber 20. The dose chamber 20 is cylindrical. The concentrate port 22 is a radial port through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 and is connected in use to a concentrate source. The carrier-liquid admission port 24 is a radial port through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 at an axial position downstream of the concentrate port 22 and admits carrier liquid to the dose chamber 20.

The piston 28 is axially slidable in the dose chamber 20 between a fill position and a discharge position. The piston 28 has an upstream sealing land 30 and a downstream sealing land 32 axially spaced from one another and joined by a reduced-diameter waist 34. Each sealing land bears on the wall of the dose chamber 20, while the waist 34 stands clear of that wall and so forms an annular space that travels with the piston 28. A piston rod 36 extends from the piston 28 along the axis of the dose chamber 20 and is arranged to be driven through a stroke and a return stroke by an external actuating member, whether a hand lever, a pneumatic or hydraulic actuator, or any other source of reciprocating motion. A one-way outlet valve 38 is arranged to pass liquid from the dose chamber 20 toward the outlet 16 and to prevent flow in the opposite direction. The one-way outlet valve 38 may take any form that passes liquid in one direction only, such as a ball or disc urged onto a seat or a resiliently biased closure element.

Ordered isolation and metering

FIG. 2 shows the piston 28 in the fill position. In the fill position the waist 34 connects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20, and the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 isolate the carrier-liquid admission port 24 from the concentrate port 22. Concentrate accordingly passes from the concentrate source through the concentrate port 22 and into the dose chamber 20, where it occupies the annular space at the waist 34 and forms a measured volume of concentrate. Throughout the fill position the carrier-liquid path is closed to the concentrate, because the downstream sealing land 32 overlies the carrier-liquid admission port 24 and the upstream sealing land 30 closes the dose chamber 20 on the other side of the waist 34.

Movement of the piston 28 toward the discharge position closes the concentrate port 22 before the downstream sealing land 32 uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port 24. The upstream sealing land 30 arrives at the concentrate port 22 and shuts it while the downstream sealing land 32 is still overlying the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Only after that has happened does continued travel of the piston 28 carry the downstream sealing land 32 clear of the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Carrier liquid then enters through the carrier-liquid admission port 24 behind the measured volume of concentrate in the dose chamber 20 and expels the measured volume through the one-way outlet valve 38 toward the outlet 16, where it joins the main flow.

The axial ordering of the faces of the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 relative to the edges of the concentrate port 22 and the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is chosen so that the concentrate port 22 is closed at every piston position at which the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is open. There is accordingly no position of the piston 28 at which the concentrate source communicates directly with the carrier-liquid path. The separation of the two liquids is a property of the geometry of the piston 28 and the metering sleeve 18 and does not depend on the order in which any external command is given, on any control signal, or on the correct operation of any separately actuated shut-off element. A slow stroke, an interrupted stroke or a stroke reversed part way through cannot open both ports at once, because the port that must close does so at an earlier point on the same continuous path of travel than the port that then opens.

Dose selection by the index collar

Referring to FIG. 4, an index collar 40 surrounds the metering sleeve 18 and has a helical cam groove 42 engaged by a follower pin 44 carried by the piston rod 36. Each full stroke of the piston 28 draws the follower pin 44 along the helical cam groove 42 and turns the index collar 40 by one increment, so that the index collar 40 advances by itself as the valve is used and needs no separate indexing drive.

Three selectable axial stop faces 46 are carried by the index collar 40 at different axial positions. The stop face presented by the current increment of rotation limits the travel of the piston 28 and thereby sets the dose volume, so that the three axial stop faces 46 correspond to three dose volumes. A spring-biased detent 48 engages one of three detent recesses 50 to retain the selected setting, so that the index collar 40 is held against vibration and against the forces transmitted through the follower pin 44 until it is next indexed.

A transparent window 52 in the housing 12 shows one of three dose setting indicia 54 carried by the index collar 40. The dose setting indicium presented at the transparent window 52 is the one associated with the axial stop face currently limiting the travel of the piston 28, so the dose setting is mechanically visible without electronics, without power at the valve and without a controller. What the window shows is the position of the mechanism itself rather than a stored value, so the displayed setting cannot disagree with the volume the valve will deliver.

Wiping and automatic rinse

FIG. 3 shows the metering portion during the return stroke of the piston 28 toward the fill position. A flexible lip 56 is carried on the upstream sealing land 30 and bears on the wall of the dose chamber 20. As the return stroke begins, the flexible lip 56 wipes the wall of the dose chamber 20 and carries the film of concentrate remaining on that wall ahead of it, so that the rinse that follows is presented with a wetted surface rather than with standing liquid.

An annular rinse channel 60 lies between an outer surface of the metering sleeve 18 and an inner surface of the housing 12 and is supplied with carrier liquid from the inlet 14. Two radial rinse openings 62 pass through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 and connect the annular rinse channel 60 to the dose chamber 20. One of the two radial rinse openings 62 is directed across the concentrate port 22 and the other is directed across the one-way outlet valve 38. These are the two surfaces on which concentrate is otherwise retained after a dose, the first because concentrate stands in the mouth of the port and the second because concentrate is the last liquid to pass the seat.

A normally closed flush poppet 58 is connected to the flush bypass 26. Near the end of the return stroke, the follower pin 44 reaches the flush poppet 58 and opens it. Carrier liquid then flows from the inlet 14 through the annular rinse channel 60, through the two radial rinse openings 62 across the concentrate port 22 and the one-way outlet valve 38, and through the flush bypass 26 to the outlet 16. The rinse liquid therefore leaves by the same route as the dose and is carried away in the main flow.

The flush poppet 58 closes before the waist 34 reconnects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20. The concentrate port 22 is closed throughout the interval in which the annular rinse channel 60 communicates with the flush bypass 26, so that carrier liquid under the pressure of the main line is never presented to an open concentrate port and cannot be driven back toward the concentrate source. Only when the flush poppet 58 has closed does the continuing return of the piston 28 bring the waist 34 back into register with the concentrate port 22, at which point the dose chamber 20 is charged again for the next dose.

Because the follower pin 44 that opens the flush poppet 58 is carried by the piston rod 36, the rinse happens once for every dose and at the same point in every cycle. It is not a separate operation, it needs no command, and it cannot be omitted while the valve continues to be used. The rinse also occurs while the concentrate port 22 is shut and after the wall of the dose chamber 20 has been wiped, so it removes a film with clean carrier liquid rather than diluting a standing charge of concentrate.

Cartridge and service

Referring again to FIG. 1, the cartridge 64 contains the piston 28, the metering sleeve 18, the one-way outlet valve 38 and the flush poppet 58, and is retained in the housing 12 by the threaded end cap 66. Removing the threaded end cap 66 withdraws the cartridge 64 from the housing 12 along the axis of the dose chamber 20 without disturbing the connections at the inlet 14 and the outlet 16, so that the wearing and sealing parts can be replaced as a unit while the housing 12 remains in the line. The parts of the cartridge 64 that contact the concentrate are the parts that are exchanged, so a change of concentrate or a worn sealing land is dealt with by fitting a further cartridge rather than by dismantling the installation.

The materials of the metering sleeve 18, the piston 28, the flexible lip 56 and the sealing elements are selected for compatibility with the carrier liquid and with the concentrate to be dosed. The spring-biased detent 48 may be a spring-loaded ball or a spring-loaded plunger, and the flexible lip 56 may be formed integrally with the upstream sealing land 30 or as a separate resilient element retained on it.

Operation

In use, carrier liquid flows through the housing 12 from the inlet 14 to the outlet 16. With the piston 28 in the fill position, concentrate is admitted through the concentrate port 22 and past the waist 34 into the dose chamber 20 to form a measured volume, the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 isolating the carrier-liquid admission port 24 from the concentrate port 22. The piston 28 is then advanced toward the discharge position so as to close the concentrate port 22 and thereafter to uncover the carrier-liquid admission port 24 with the downstream sealing land 32. Carrier liquid is admitted through the carrier-liquid admission port 24 behind the measured volume and expels the measured volume through the one-way outlet valve 38 toward the outlet 16. The travel of the piston 28 on this stroke is limited by the selected one of the three axial stop faces 46, which sets the measured volume.

The piston 28 is then returned toward the fill position. During the return, the flexible lip 56 on the upstream sealing land 30 wipes the wall of the dose chamber 20, and the follower pin 44 carried by the piston rod 36 opens the normally closed flush poppet 58. Carrier liquid flows through the annular rinse channel 60 between the metering sleeve 18 and the housing 12, through the two radial rinse openings 62 in the metering sleeve 18 across the concentrate port 22 and the one-way outlet valve 38, and through the flush bypass 26 that opens downstream of the dose chamber 20 to the outlet 16. The flush poppet 58 is closed before the waist 34 reconnects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20. Over the same full stroke, the follower pin 44 travelling in the helical cam groove 42 turns the index collar 40 by one increment, the spring-biased detent 48 enters the next of the three detent recesses 50, and the dose setting indicium then presented at the transparent window 52 shows the setting that will govern the next dose. The valve is thereby left charged, rinsed and set, ready for the following cycle.

The foregoing description sets out embodiments of the invention. A skilled reader may make changes of detail to the described embodiments without departing from the scope of the claims that follow.

In the following description, the terms upstream and downstream refer to the direction of travel of the carrier liquid from the inlet toward the outlet, and the terms axial and radial refer to the axis along which the piston slides.

Overall arrangement

FIG. 1 shows an inline liquid metering valve 10 having a cylindrical housing 12 with an inlet 14 at one axial end and an outlet 16 at the opposite axial end, a metering sleeve 18 fixed within the housing 12, a cartridge 64 retained in the housing 12 by a threaded end cap 66, and a transparent window 52 in the housing 12.

The inline liquid metering valve 10 is connected in a line that already carries a flowing carrier liquid. Carrier liquid enters at the inlet 14, passes along the housing 12, and leaves at the outlet 16. That flow is the main flow into which each dose of concentrate is delivered, and it is also the only liquid used to rinse the valve. The metering sleeve 18 is spaced radially inward from the inner surface of the housing 12 over part of its length.

Metering sleeve, ports and piston

FIG. 2 shows the metering sleeve 18, which defines a dose chamber 20, a concentrate port 22 opening into the dose chamber 20 and a carrier-liquid admission port 24 opening into the dose chamber 20, together with an upstream sealing land 30 and a downstream sealing land 32 joined by a reduced-diameter waist 34, and a one-way outlet valve 38.

The dose chamber 20 is cylindrical. The concentrate port 22 is a radial port through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 and is connected in use to a concentrate source. The carrier-liquid admission port 24 is a radial port through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 at an axial position downstream of the concentrate port 22, and admits carrier liquid to the dose chamber 20. The metering sleeve 18 further defines a flush bypass 26 that opens downstream of the dose chamber 20.

A piston 28 is axially slidable in the dose chamber 20 between a fill position and a discharge position. The upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 are axially spaced from one another on the piston 28 and are joined by the reduced-diameter waist 34. Each sealing land bears on the wall of the dose chamber 20, while the waist 34 stands clear of that wall and so forms an annular space that travels with the piston 28. A piston rod 36 extends from the piston 28 along the axis of the dose chamber 20 and is arranged to be driven through a stroke and a return stroke by an external actuating member, whether a hand lever, a pneumatic or hydraulic actuator, or another source of reciprocating motion. The one-way outlet valve 38 is arranged to pass liquid from the dose chamber 20 toward the outlet 16 and to prevent flow in the opposite direction. The one-way outlet valve 38 may take any form that passes liquid in one direction only, such as a ball or a disc urged onto a seat, or a resiliently biased closure element.

Ordered isolation and metering

In the fill position the waist 34 connects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20, and the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 isolate the carrier-liquid admission port 24 from the concentrate port 22. Concentrate accordingly passes from the concentrate source through the concentrate port 22 into the dose chamber 20, where it occupies the annular space at the waist 34 and forms a measured volume of concentrate. Throughout the fill position the carrier-liquid path is closed to the concentrate, because the downstream sealing land 32 overlies the carrier-liquid admission port 24 while the upstream sealing land 30 closes the dose chamber 20 on the other side of the waist 34.

Movement of the piston 28 toward the discharge position closes the concentrate port 22 before the downstream sealing land 32 uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port 24. The upstream sealing land 30 arrives at the concentrate port 22 and shuts it while the downstream sealing land 32 is still overlying the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Only after that has happened does continued travel of the piston 28 carry the downstream sealing land 32 clear of the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Carrier liquid then enters through the carrier-liquid admission port 24 behind the measured volume of concentrate in the dose chamber 20 and expels the measured volume through the one-way outlet valve 38 toward the outlet 16, where it joins the main flow.

The axial ordering of the faces of the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 relative to the edges of the concentrate port 22 and the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is chosen so that the concentrate port 22 is closed at every position of the piston 28 at which the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is open. There is accordingly no position of the piston 28 at which the concentrate source communicates directly with the carrier-liquid path. The separation of the two liquids is a property of the geometry of the piston 28 and the metering sleeve 18. It does not depend on the order in which external commands are given, on any control signal, or on the correct operation of a separately actuated shut-off element. A slow stroke, an interrupted stroke, or a stroke reversed part way through cannot open both ports at once, because the port that must close does so at an earlier point on the same continuous path of travel than the point at which the other port opens.

Dose selection by the index collar

FIG. 4 shows an index collar 40 having a helical cam groove 42 engaged by a follower pin 44 carried by the piston rod 36, three selectable axial stop faces 46, a spring-biased detent 48 engaging one of three detent recesses 50, and three dose setting indicia 54.

The index collar 40 surrounds the metering sleeve 18. Each full stroke of the piston 28 draws the follower pin 44 along the helical cam groove 42 and turns the index collar 40 by one increment, so that the index collar 40 advances by itself as the valve is used and needs no separate indexing drive.

The three axial stop faces 46 are carried by the index collar 40 at different axial positions. The stop face presented by the current increment of rotation limits the travel of the piston 28 and thereby sets the dose volume, so that the three axial stop faces 46 correspond to three dose volumes. The spring-biased detent 48 engages one of the three detent recesses 50 to retain the selected setting, so that the index collar 40 is held against vibration and against the forces transmitted through the follower pin 44 until it is next indexed.

The transparent window 52 in the housing 12 shows one of the three dose setting indicia 54 carried by the index collar 40. The dose setting indicium presented at the transparent window 52 is the one associated with the axial stop face then limiting the travel of the piston 28, so that the dose setting is mechanically visible without electronics, without power at the valve and without a controller. What is seen at the transparent window 52 is the position of the mechanism itself rather than a stored value, so the displayed setting cannot disagree with the volume that the valve will deliver.

Wiping and automatic rinse

FIG. 3 shows the piston 28 during the return stroke toward the fill position, with a flexible lip 56, a follower pin 44 holding a flush poppet 58 open, an annular rinse channel 60, two radial rinse openings 62 leading toward the concentrate port 22, and a flush bypass 26.

The flexible lip 56 is carried on the upstream sealing land 30 and bears on the wall of the dose chamber 20. As the return stroke begins, the flexible lip 56 wipes the wall of the dose chamber 20 and carries the film of concentrate remaining on that wall ahead of it, so that the rinse which follows is presented with a wetted surface rather than with standing liquid.

The annular rinse channel 60 lies between an outer surface of the metering sleeve 18 and an inner surface of the housing 12, and is supplied with carrier liquid from the inlet 14. The two radial rinse openings 62 pass through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 and connect the annular rinse channel 60 to the dose chamber 20. One of the two radial rinse openings 62 is directed across the concentrate port 22 and the other is directed across the one-way outlet valve 38. Those are the two surfaces on which concentrate is otherwise retained after a dose, the first because concentrate stands in the mouth of the port and the second because concentrate is the last liquid to pass the seat.

The flush poppet 58 is normally closed and is connected to the flush bypass 26. Near the end of the return stroke, the follower pin 44 reaches the flush poppet 58 and opens it. Carrier liquid then flows from the inlet 14 through the annular rinse channel 60, through the two radial rinse openings 62 across the concentrate port 22 and the one-way outlet valve 38, and through the flush bypass 26 to the outlet 16. The rinse liquid therefore leaves by the same route as the dose and is carried away in the main flow.

The flush poppet 58 closes before the waist 34 reconnects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20. The concentrate port 22 is closed throughout the interval in which the annular rinse channel 60 communicates with the flush bypass 26, so that carrier liquid at the pressure of the main line is never presented to an open concentrate port 22 and cannot be driven back toward the concentrate source. Only when the flush poppet 58 has closed does the continuing return of the piston 28 bring the waist 34 back into register with the concentrate port 22, at which point the dose chamber 20 is charged again for the next dose.

Because the follower pin 44 that opens the flush poppet 58 is carried by the piston rod 36, the rinse occurs once for every dose and at the same point in every cycle. It is not a separate operation, it needs no command, and it cannot be omitted while the valve continues to be used. The rinse also occurs while the concentrate port 22 is shut and after the wall of the dose chamber 20 has been wiped, so that it removes a film with clean carrier liquid instead of diluting a standing charge of concentrate.

Cartridge and service

The cartridge 64 contains the piston 28, the metering sleeve 18, the one-way outlet valve 38 and the flush poppet 58. Removing the threaded end cap 66 withdraws the cartridge 64 from the housing 12 along the axis of the dose chamber 20 without disturbing the connections at the inlet 14 and the outlet 16, so that the wearing and sealing parts are replaced as a unit while the housing 12 remains in the line. The parts that contact the concentrate are the parts that are exchanged, so a change of concentrate or a worn sealing land is dealt with by fitting a further cartridge rather than by dismantling the installation.

Carrier liquid is admitted through the carrier-liquid admission port 24 behind the measured volume and expels the measured volume through the one-way outlet valve 38 toward the outlet 16. The travel of the piston 28 on this stroke is limited by the selected one of the three axial stop faces 46, which sets the measured volume.

The piston 28 is then returned toward the fill position. During the return, the flexible lip 56 on the upstream sealing land 30 wipes the wall of the dose chamber 20, and the follower pin 44 carried by the piston rod 36 opens the normally closed flush poppet 58. Carrier liquid flows through the annular rinse channel 60 between the metering sleeve 18 and the housing 12, through the two radial rinse openings 62 in the metering sleeve 18 across the concentrate port 22 and the one-way outlet valve 38, and through the flush bypass 26 that opens downstream of the dose chamber 20 to the outlet 16. The flush poppet 58 is closed before the waist 34 reconnects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20. Over the same full stroke, the follower pin 44 travelling in the helical cam groove 42 turns the index collar 40 by one increment, the spring-biased detent 48 enters the next of the three detent recesses 50, and the dose setting indicium then presented at the transparent window 52 shows the setting that will govern the next dose. The valve is thereby left charged, rinsed and set, ready for the following cycle.

# FIG. 1

View: longitudinal sectional view of the complete inline liquid metering valve, axis horizontal. All line work lies well inside the drawing area, clear of the sheet edges and filing margins.

Geometry:

- The housing is an elongate cylinder cut lengthwise on its axis, appearing as an upper hatched wall band and a lower hatched wall band running across most of the width of the drawing area and joined at the right by a hatched end wall. The interior between the bands is open.
- The left end of the housing is closed by a threaded end cap, drawn as a short hatched ring seated in the left mouth of the housing, its outer surface meeting the housing bore along a shallow saw-tooth interface indicating a thread. A plain shaft lies on the axis, passes through the central opening of the ring and projects to the left of it, ending clear of the drawing area boundary.
- A short tubular stub projects downward from the lower housing wall band near the left end and opens into the housing interior; it is the inlet, shown schematically. A second such stub projects downward near the right end and opens into the housing interior; it is the outlet, shown schematically. Both stubs end clear of the drawing area boundary.
- The metering sleeve lies inside the housing on the same axis, drawn as an upper hatched band and a lower hatched band spaced inward from the housing wall bands, so that a clear gap is visible above and below it along its length. It extends from a position right of the end cap to a position short of the housing end wall.
- At its left end the metering sleeve carries an annular flange, drawn as a taller hatched block above and below the axis, abutting the inner face of the end cap. The flange and the sleeve together represent the removable cartridge.
- Within the sleeve bore, in the left half, is a body shown schematically as two hatched enlarged portions joined by a narrower hatched middle portion. The plain shaft runs from the left enlarged portion out through the end cap.
- A rectangular unhatched panel is set into the upper housing wall band about midway along its length, the wall hatching stopping at the panel outline. The panel is the transparent window. Beneath it, on the upper surface of an unnumbered ring surrounding the metering sleeve in the clear gap, a small plain patch is visible.

Numerals on this sheet: 10, 12, 14, 16, 18, 52, 64, 66.

Targets:

- 10: the complete assembly; leader ends just outside the upper outline of the housing, above the left half.
- 12: the hatched lower housing wall band, well inside the hatching at mid length.
- 14: the wall of the left downward stub.
- 16: the wall of the right downward stub.
- 18: the hatched upper band of the metering sleeve, toward its right.
- 52: the interior of the unhatched rectangular panel.
- 64: the hatched flange at the left end of the sleeve, above the axis.
- 66: the hatched ring closing the left mouth of the housing, above the axis.

# FIG. 2

View: enlarged longitudinal sectional view of the metering portion of the valve of FIG. 1, axis horizontal, with the piston in the fill position. All line work lies well inside the drawing area, clear of the sheet edges and filing margins.

Geometry:

- The metering sleeve is cut lengthwise on its axis and appears as an upper hatched wall band and a lower hatched wall band running across the width of the drawing area. The open space between them is the cylindrical dose chamber.
- In the left portion of that space, an upstream sealing land is drawn as a hatched block whose upper and lower edges meet the bore walls; a downstream sealing land is drawn as a second such hatched block spaced to its right; and a waist joins them, drawn as a hatched bar of smaller height on the axis, so that open space is visible between the waist and the upper bore wall and between the waist and the lower bore wall.
- A plain shaft on the axis extends leftward from the upstream sealing land and ends clear of the drawing area boundary.
- A radial opening passes through the upper wall band at an axial position between the two sealing lands, its inner mouth opening into the space above the waist. A short tube continues upward from it and ends clear of the drawing area boundary; the tube is shown schematically and represents the connection to a concentrate source. This opening is the concentrate port.
- A second radial opening passes through the lower wall band at the axial position of the downstream sealing land, its inner mouth covered by the lower edge of that land. A short tube continues downward from it and ends clear of the drawing area boundary. This opening is the carrier-liquid admission port and lies to the right of the concentrate port.
- To the right of the downstream sealing land, a further passage rises through the upper wall band and widens downward into a conical seat opening into the dose chamber, with a ball resting on the seat and closing the passage. The ball and seat are shown schematically and represent the one-way outlet valve, which passes liquid outward and upward from the dose chamber.

Numerals on this sheet: 18, 20, 22, 24, 30, 32, 34, 38.

Targets:

- 18: the hatched lower wall band of the metering sleeve, toward the right of the view.
- 20: the open space of the dose chamber above the waist, between the two sealing lands.
- 22: the interior of the radial opening in the upper wall band that opens above the waist.
- 24: the interior of the radial opening in the lower wall band that is covered by the downstream sealing land.
- 30: the hatching of the left sealing land block.
- 32: the hatching of the right sealing land block.
- 34: the hatching of the narrower bar joining the two blocks.
- 38: the ball resting on the conical seat.

# FIG. 3

View: enlarged longitudinal sectional view of the metering portion of the valve of FIG. 1 during the return stroke, axis horizontal, with the flush poppet held open. All line work lies well inside the drawing area, clear of the sheet edges and filing margins.

Geometry:

- An outer wall is cut lengthwise and appears as an upper hatched band along the top and a lower hatched band along the bottom, running across the width of the drawing area.
- Inside it, an inner tubular wall is cut lengthwise and appears as an upper hatched band and a lower hatched band spaced inward from the outer bands, beginning a short distance from the left and continuing to the right of the view. The open space between the inner bands is the bore.
- The clear gap between the lower inner band and the lower outer band is the annular rinse channel; it is closed at the left by a hatched transverse boss and runs to the right of the view. The clear gap between the upper inner band and the upper outer band is an open passage carrying liquid to the right.
- In the bore, the piston is drawn as two hatched enlarged portions joined by a narrower hatched middle portion, positioned in the left half and travelling to the left. A plain shaft extends leftward on the axis from the left enlarged portion, past the left end of the inner wall, ending clear of the drawing area boundary.
- At the left edge of the left enlarged portion, a thin flared projection extends upward and to the left to touch the upper bore wall, and a matching projection extends downward and to the left to touch the lower bore wall. These are the flexible lip.
- A short pin projects downward from the plain shaft left of the inner wall. Its lower end bears on the right end of a stem running leftward to a conical head. The head stands clear of a seat formed in an opening through the transverse boss, a visible gap separating head from seat. Head and stem are shown schematically and represent the flush poppet, held open by the pin.
- A radial opening passes through the upper inner band at a position covered by the left enlarged portion; a short tube continues upward from it, crosses the upper passage, passes through the upper outer band and ends clear of the drawing area boundary. This opening is the concentrate port.
- Two radial openings pass through the lower inner band and connect the annular rinse channel to the bore. The left one lies directly beneath the concentrate port and is aimed at it. The right one lies beneath a conical seat carrying a ball, shown schematically in a passage rising through the upper inner band in the right half, and is aimed at that seat. These are the radial rinse openings.
- Right of that ball and seat, a further opening passes through the upper inner band and connects the bore to the upper passage. It is the flush bypass and lies downstream of the piston.

Numerals on this sheet: 22, 26, 28, 44, 56, 58, 60, 62.

Targets:

- 22: the interior of the upper inner band opening covered by the left enlarged portion.
- 26: the interior of the opening through the upper inner band at the right.
- 28: the hatching of the right enlarged portion in the bore.
- 44: the short pin projecting downward from the plain shaft.
- 56: the flared projection touching the upper bore wall.
- 58: the conical head standing clear of its seat.
- 60: the clear gap between the lower bands, left of the two radial openings.
- 62: the interior of the left of the two openings through the lower inner band.

# FIG. 3

View: enlarged longitudinal sectional view of the metering portion of the valve of FIG. 1 during the return stroke, axis horizontal, with the flush poppet held open. All line work lies well inside the drawing area, clear of the sheet edges and filing margins.

Geometry:

- An outer wall is cut lengthwise and appears as an upper hatched band along the top and a lower hatched band along the bottom, running across the width of the drawing area.
- Inside it, an inner tubular wall is cut lengthwise and appears as an upper hatched band and a lower hatched band spaced inward from the outer bands, beginning a short distance from the left and continuing to the right of the view. The open space between the inner bands is the bore.
- The clear gap between the lower inner band and the lower outer band is the annular rinse channel; it is closed at the left by a hatched transverse boss and runs to the right of the view. The clear gap between the upper bands is an open passage carrying liquid to the right.
- In the bore, the piston is drawn as two hatched enlarged portions joined by a narrower hatched middle portion, in the left half of the view. A plain shaft extends leftward on the axis from the left enlarged portion, past the left end of the inner wall, ending clear of the drawing area boundary.
- At the left edge of the left enlarged portion, a thin flared projection extends upward and to the left to touch the upper bore wall, and a matching projection extends downward and to the left to touch the lower bore wall. These are the flexible lip.
- A short pin projects downward from the plain shaft left of the inner wall. Its lower end bears on the right end of a stem running leftward to a conical head. The head stands clear of a seat formed in an opening through the transverse boss, a visible gap separating head from seat. Head and stem are shown schematically and represent the flush poppet, held open by the pin.
- A radial opening passes through the upper inner band at a position covered by the left enlarged portion; a short tube continues upward from it, crosses the upper passage, passes through the upper outer band and ends clear of the drawing area boundary. This opening is the concentrate port.
- Two radial openings pass through the lower inner band and connect the annular rinse channel to the bore. The left one lies directly beneath the concentrate port and is aimed at it. The right one lies beneath a conical seat carrying a ball, shown schematically in a passage rising through the upper inner band in the right half, and is aimed at that seat. These are the radial rinse openings.
- Right of that ball and seat, a further opening through the upper inner band connects the bore to the upper passage. It is the flush bypass.

Numerals on this sheet: 22, 26, 28, 44, 56, 58, 60, 62.

Targets:

- 22: the interior of the upper inner band opening covered by the left enlarged portion.
- 26: the interior of the opening through the upper inner band at the right.
- 28: the hatching of the right enlarged portion in the bore.
- 44: the short pin projecting downward from the plain shaft.
- 56: the flared projection touching the upper bore wall.
- 58: the conical head standing clear of its seat.
- 60: the clear gap between the lower bands, left of the two radial openings.
- 62: the interior of the left of the two openings through the lower inner band.

1	In the following description, the terms upstream and downstream refer to the direction of travel of the carrier liquid from the inlet toward the outlet, and the terms axial and radial refer to the axis along which the piston slides.
2	
3	Overall arrangement
4	
5	FIG. 1 shows an inline liquid metering valve 10 having a cylindrical housing 12 with an inlet 14 at one axial end and an outlet 16 at the opposite axial end, a metering sleeve 18 fixed within the housing 12, a cartridge 64 retained in the housing 12 by a threaded end cap 66, and a transparent window 52 in the housing 12.
6	
7	The inline liquid metering valve 10 is connected in a line that already carries a flowing carrier liquid. Carrier liquid enters at the inlet 14, passes along the housing 12, and leaves at the outlet 16. That flow is the main flow into which each dose of concentrate is delivered, and it is also the only liquid used to rinse the valve. The metering sleeve 18 is spaced radially inward from the inner surface of the housing 12 over part of its length.
8	
9	Metering sleeve, ports and piston
10	
11	FIG. 2 shows the metering sleeve 18 defining a dose chamber 20, a concentrate port 22 opening into the dose chamber 20 and a carrier-liquid admission port 24 opening into the dose chamber 20. FIG. 2 further shows an upstream sealing land 30 and a downstream sealing land 32 joined by a reduced-diameter waist 34 in the fill position, and a one-way outlet valve 38.
12	
13	The dose chamber 20 is cylindrical. The concentrate port 22 is a radial port through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 and is connected in use to a concentrate source. The carrier-liquid admission port 24 is a radial port through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 at an axial position downstream of the concentrate port 22, and admits carrier liquid to the dose chamber 20. The metering sleeve 18 further defines a flush bypass 26 that opens downstream of the dose chamber 20.
14	
15	A piston 28 is axially slidable in the dose chamber 20 between a fill position and a discharge position. The upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 are axially spaced from one another on the piston 28 and are joined by the reduced-diameter waist 34. Each sealing land bears on the wall of the dose chamber 20, while the waist 34 stands clear of that wall and so forms an annular space that travels with the piston 28. A piston rod 36 extends from the piston 28 along the axis of the dose chamber 20 and is arranged to be driven through a stroke and a return stroke by an external actuating member, whether a hand lever, a pneumatic or hydraulic actuator, or another source of reciprocating motion. The one-way outlet valve 38 is arranged to pass liquid from the dose chamber 20 toward the outlet 16 and to prevent flow in the opposite direction. The one-way outlet valve 38 may take any form that passes liquid in one direction only, such as a ball or a disc urged onto a seat, or a resiliently biased closure element.
16	
17	Ordered isolation and metering
18	
19	In the fill position the waist 34 connects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20, and the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 isolate the carrier-liquid admission port 24 from the concentrate port 22. Concentrate accordingly passes from the concentrate source through the concentrate port 22 into the dose chamber 20, where it occupies the annular space at the waist 34 and forms a measured volume of concentrate. Throughout the fill position the carrier-liquid path is closed to the concentrate, because the downstream sealing land 32 overlies the carrier-liquid admission port 24 while the upstream sealing land 30 closes the dose chamber 20 on the other side of the waist 34.
20	
21	Movement of the piston 28 toward the discharge position closes the concentrate port 22 before the downstream sealing land 32 uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port 24. The upstream sealing land 30 arrives at the concentrate port 22 and shuts it while the downstream sealing land 32 is still overlying the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Only after that has happened does continued travel of the piston 28 carry the downstream sealing land 32 clear of the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Carrier liquid then enters through the carrier-liquid admission port 24 behind the measured volume of concentrate in the dose chamber 20 and expels the measured volume through the one-way outlet valve 38 toward the outlet 16, where it joins the main flow.
22	
23	The axial ordering of the faces of the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 relative to the edges of the concentrate port 22 and the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is chosen so that the concentrate port 22 is closed at every position of the piston 28 at which the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is open. There is accordingly no position of the piston 28 at which the concentrate source communicates directly with the carrier-liquid path. The separation of the two liquids is a property of the geometry of the piston 28 and the metering sleeve 18. It does not depend on the order in which external commands are given, on any control signal, or on the correct operation of a separately actuated shut-off element. A slow stroke, an interrupted stroke, or a stroke reversed part way through cannot open both ports at once, because the port that must close does so at an earlier point on the same continuous path of travel than the point at which the other port opens.
24	
25	Dose selection by the index collar
26	
27	FIG. 4 shows an index collar 40 having a helical cam groove 42 engaged by a follower pin 44 carried by the piston rod 36, three selectable axial stop faces 46, a spring-biased detent 48 engaging one of three detent recesses 50, and three dose setting indicia 54.
28	
29	The index collar 40 surrounds the metering sleeve 18. Each full stroke of the piston 28 draws the follower pin 44 along the helical cam groove 42 and turns the index collar 40 by one increment, so that the index collar 40 advances by itself as the valve is used and needs no separate indexing drive.
30	
31	The three axial stop faces 46 are carried by the index collar 40 at different axial positions. The stop face presented by the current increment of rotation limits the travel of the piston 28 and thereby sets the dose volume, so that the three axial stop faces 46 correspond to three dose volumes. The spring-biased detent 48 engages one of the three detent recesses 50 to retain the selected setting, so that the index collar 40 is held against vibration and against the forces transmitted through the follower pin 44 until it is next indexed.
32	
33	The transparent window 52 in the housing 12 shows one of the three dose setting indicia 54 carried by the index collar 40. The dose setting indicium presented at the transparent window 52 is the one associated with the axial stop face then limiting the travel of the piston 28, so that the dose setting is mechanically visible without electronics, without power at the valve and without a controller. What is seen at the transparent window 52 is the position of the mechanism itself rather than a stored value, so the displayed setting cannot disagree with the volume that the valve will deliver.
34	
35	Wiping and automatic rinse
36	
37	FIG. 3 shows the piston 28 during the return stroke toward the fill position, with a flexible lip 56, the follower pin 44 holding a flush poppet 58 open, an annular rinse channel 60, two radial rinse openings 62 leading toward the concentrate port 22, and a flush bypass 26.
38	
39	The flexible lip 56 is carried on the upstream sealing land 30 and bears on the wall of the dose chamber 20. As the return stroke begins, the flexible lip 56 wipes the wall of the dose chamber 20 and carries the film of concentrate remaining on that wall ahead of it, so that the rinse which follows is presented with a wetted surface rather than with standing liquid.

A piston rod 36 extends from the piston 28 along the axis of the dose chamber 20 and is arranged to be driven through a stroke and a return stroke by an external actuating member, whether a hand lever, a pneumatic or hydraulic actuator, or another source of reciprocating motion. The one-way outlet valve 38 is arranged to pass liquid from the dose chamber 20 toward the outlet 16 and to prevent flow in the opposite direction. The one-way outlet valve 38 may take any form that passes liquid in one direction only, such as a ball or a disc urged onto a seat, or a resiliently biased closure element.

In the fill position the waist 34 connects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20, and the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 isolate the carrier-liquid admission port 24 from the concentrate port 22. Concentrate accordingly passes from the concentrate source through the concentrate port 22 into the dose chamber 20, where it occupies the annular space at the waist 34 and forms a measured volume of concentrate. Throughout the fill position the carrier-liquid path is closed to the concentrate, because the downstream sealing land 32 overlies the carrier-liquid admission port 24 while the upstream sealing land 30 closes the dose chamber 20 on the other side of the waist 34.

The axial ordering of the faces of the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 relative to the edges of the concentrate port 22 and the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is chosen so that the concentrate port 22 is closed at every position of the piston 28 at which the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is open. There is accordingly no position of the piston 28 at which the concentrate source communicates directly with the carrier-liquid path. The separation of the two liquids is a property of the geometry of the piston 28 and the metering sleeve 18. It does not depend on the order in which external commands are given, on any control signal, or on the correct operation of a separately actuated shut-off element. A slow stroke, an interrupted stroke, or a stroke reversed part way through cannot open both ports at once, because the port that must close does so at an earlier point on the same continuous path of travel than the point at which the other port opens.

FIG. 4 shows an index collar 40 having a helical cam groove 42 engaged by a follower pin 44 carried by the piston rod 36, three selectable axial stop faces 46, a spring-biased detent 48 engaging one of three detent recesses 50, and three dose setting indicia 54.

The index collar 40 surrounds the metering sleeve 18. Each full stroke of the piston 28 draws the follower pin 44 along the helical cam groove 42 and turns the index collar 40 by one increment, so that the index collar 40 advances by itself as the valve is used and needs no separate indexing drive.

The three axial stop faces 46 are carried by the index collar 40 at different axial positions. The stop face presented by the current increment of rotation limits the travel of the piston 28 and thereby sets the dose volume, so that the three axial stop faces 46 correspond to three dose volumes. The spring-biased detent 48 engages one of the three detent recesses 50 to retain the selected setting, so that the index collar 40 is held against vibration and against the forces transmitted through the follower pin 44 until it is next indexed.

The dose setting indicium presented at the transparent window 52 is the one associated with the axial stop face then limiting the travel of the piston 28, so that the dose setting is mechanically visible without electronics, without power at the valve and without a controller. What is seen at the transparent window 52 is the position of the mechanism itself rather than a stored value, so the displayed setting cannot disagree with the volume that the valve will deliver.

FIG. 3 shows the piston 28 during the return stroke toward the fill position, with a flexible lip 56, the follower pin 44 holding a flush poppet 58 open, an annular rinse channel 60, two radial rinse openings 62 leading toward the concentrate port 22, and a flush bypass 26.

The flexible lip 56 is carried on the upstream sealing land 30 and bears on the wall of the dose chamber 20. input.summary: Wrote the complete first draft of the application for the self-flushing inline liquid metering valve: all ten draft/ body files, a 29-entry numeral table, and four figure specifications (whole-valve section, metering-detail section in the fill position, rinse-detail section on the return stroke, and an index-collar detail). Claims are 20 in two statutory classes: apparatus claim 1 with dependents 2 to 12, and method claim 13 with dependents 14 to 20. Note on the art: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so the Background carries no citations and the art you gave me may be incomplete; the claims were drafted against the disclosure and the general problem statement rather than against searched references, and a real search could change what claim 1 should recite.
reasoning: Claim 1 recites three ordered relationships rather than one, because the ordering is what the invention actually is: the concentrate port closes before the downstream land uncovers the admission port, and the follower pin on the piston rod opens the flush poppet on the return stroke with the poppet closing before the waist reconnects the concentrate port. A spool with two lands and a waist, a check valve on the outlet, and a rinse line are each ordinary in isolation; what is not ordinary is that the rinse is gated by the element that carries the metering piston, so the rinse cannot be commanded late, skipped, or performed while the concentrate port is open. That coupling is the feature I would argue from, and it is stated in the Summary and the Detailed Description before it is needed.

I deliberately kept the whole indexing mechanism out of claim 1. The index collar, helical cam groove, three stop faces, detent, window and indicia are the most visually distinctive part of the disclosure, but none of them is needed to make the metering and self-rinse sequence work, so putting them in claim 1 would have given away scope for nothing. They form the second rung of the ladder at claims 6 to 9 and 17 to 19, where each adds a feature that can be argued on its own: self-indexing from the stroke, travel-limited dose volumes, mechanical retention, and mechanical display.

Claim 1 says 'at least one rinse opening' although the disclosure describes two. The two-opening arrangement, with one aimed across the concentrate port and one across the one-way outlet valve, is the version that solves the residue problem the Background sets up, so it sits in claims 2 and 15 as the next-narrowest fallback rather than as a limitation on the broadest claim.

Claims 4, 5 and 16 exist as separate rungs because they capture the two consequences of the geometry that are easiest to defend and hardest to design around: no piston position places the concentrate source in communication with the carrier path, and the concentrate port stays shut throughout the rinse interval. Both are supported in the same words in the Detailed Description.

The cartridge and threaded end cap are claimed at 10, 11 and 20 rather than in claim 1. They are a serviceability embodiment and a different infringement story (the replacement cartridge itself), so they belong in their own rung, and the method claim ends with the cartridge exchange step for that reason.

The disclosure fixes the ordering of the ports and lands but not the axial location of the flush poppet, the direction the piston travels to discharge, or how the rod is driven. I resolved only what the drawings could not avoid resolving, and I resolved it in the figure briefs rather than in the specification: the spec says the poppet is normally closed and connected to the flush bypass and that the pin opens it near the end of the return, while the drawing places the poppet where the pin can physically reach it. No invented location, dimension, material value, or performance figure entered the patent text or the claims.

Numerals were allocated to keep every sheet at or under eight. FIG. 1 carries the assembly, housing, ports, sleeve, window, cartridge and end cap; FIG. 2 carries the metering geometry; FIG. 3 carries the rinse circuit; FIG. 4 carries the indexing parts. Where a part had to appear on a sheet that does not number it, the brief describes it generically as a hatched band, a plain shaft, an unnumbered ring or a ball on a seat, so no figure shows a part it does not list. Figure references in the Detailed Description were rewritten so that each 'FIG. n shows' sentence names only numerals that appear on that sheet.

The external concentrate source was left unnumbered. It is not part of the valve, it is drawn only as a short schematic stub that ends inside the drawing area, and numbering it would have cost a slot on a sheet that needed it for claimed structure.

The Background carries no citations because prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references. It states the technical problems in neutral terms, carryover residue between doses, dependence on command ordering for liquid separation, and the fragility of screw or electronic dose settings, so that the later arguments about the ordered port geometry and the stroke-driven rinse have somewhere in the specification to attach.
